title: Mere Christianity
author: C.S. Lewis
edition_analyzed: HarperOne, 2001 (standard modern edition; content based on original BBC radio talks from 1941–1944, first collected in book form in 1952)
target_audience: Agnostics and skeptics interested in Christianity
General readers interested in philosophy, ethics, or religion
core_themes: The moral law and the existence of God
The nature of faith, hope, and charity
primary_purpose: To clearly present and defend the core teachings and moral concepts of Christianity to a broad, lay audience, avoiding doctrinal disputes and focusing on the essentials shared by most denominations.

structure_format.narrative_style: Conversational, logical, accessible, and reasoned; originally delivered as radio broadcasts, retaining an oral and engaging tone.
structure_format.organization: Divided into four books: Right and Wrong as a Clue to the Meaning of the Universe; What Christians Believe; Christian Behaviour; and Beyond Personality: Or First Steps in the Doctrine of the Trinity.
features: Emphasis on universal Christianity, not denominational specifics

key_concepts_lessons: All humans possess an innate sense of right and wrong, pointing to a universal ‘moral law’ and suggesting a Moral Lawgiver (God).
Christianity provides coherent explanations for human morality, sin, and the need for redemption.
Christian faith centers on the person and work of Jesus Christ.
True Christian living goes beyond belief to ethical behavior: charity, forgiveness, humility, and hope.
Spiritual transformation (‘becoming a new person’) is essential and possible only through Christ.
Unity among Christian denominations is important; ‘mere’ Christianity seeks to define the core beliefs they share.
notable_features: Adaptation of BBC radio talks during WWII
Widely accessible explanations with memorable analogies
Frequently cited for its clear defense of Christian basics
cultural_historical_context: Originating as a series of BBC radio broadcasts during the Second World War, Mere Christianity sought to offer hope and clarity to a British population shaken by war and uncertainty. The book is set against a backdrop of skepticism, post-war searching, and denominational fragmentation, aiming to unite Christians and introduce nonbelievers to the faith’s logical foundation.
reception_impact: Regarded as one of the most significant works of Christian apologetics in the 20th century
Inspired countless readers—believers and seekers alike—to consider or embrace Christianity
Praised for its lucidity, humility, and logical approach
Influences both Protestant and Catholic circles; still widely read and cited
Some critics find its arguments unconvincing or dated, and note limitations in addressing non-Western perspectives
comparable_titles: The Case for Christ by Lee Strobel
The Reason for God by Timothy Keller
The Screwtape Letters by C.S. Lewis
Mere Apologetics by Alister E. McGrath
